doc.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013

title: Art Tatum's solo concert at Brandeis
summary: Morgenstern brings Tatum to Brandeis, writes his first jazz piece, and Tatum says it was his first solo concert, inspiring him to work for the music.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Art Tatum: the legend, the piano and the man

blocks.x: downstairs called Mahogany Hall, which was the traditional club, and upstairs was Storyville, and on Sunday afternoons both bands would play. And then at the end there would be some get-together. So the most remarkable thing that involved that kind of a Sunday afternoon was when Art Tatum’s trio was upstairs and Sidney Bechet was downstairs. And for the jam they got together and played as Sidney sat in with the Tatum trio, and they played “Lady Be Good” and that was a [gestures]. This was on the occasion — that was also the real coup. We brought Stan Getz — he had Brookmeyer — we brought them to campus And that was very nice but there was no — I became friendly with Stan later, much later. But it was very, you know, it was kind of impersonal. They came, they played, they played very well, the students liked it, but that was in and out. But then we wanted to get Tatum, and I really wanted Tatum without the trio. I wanted him to do a solo. And we went to talk to him and he immediately said yes. And so we were able to bring Tatum. Brandeis is about 16 miles out of Boston, you know, it’s in Waltham, it’s easy to get to. And we got the best piano on campus and got it tuned to a tee and everything. We picked him up in Boston and drove him to campus and he played a marvelous concert. One of the people who showed up was Machito, who happened to be somewhere in the area and he found out about it.

The leader of that great Latin band, which you know Charlie Parker recorded with them and everybody. Frank Grillo was his real name. And all the classical people at — Brandeis had a pretty heavy classical faculty with some fairly well known composers — and they all came to see Tatum. And he played a marvelous concert. DownBeat had a correspondent then, Nat Hentoff had left already, and that was Dom Cerulli. He reviewed it for DownBeat actually. This was in 1955, the year before Tatum died. And this was, you know, in order to get people to come to these things I would write something in the paper about them, and that was really my first jazz writing. And then when we drove Tatum back to Boston I was sitting with him in the back and my friends were driving. And I said to him, you know, I thanked him. And he said, “I should thank you,” he said, “because” — and this totally overwhelmed me — he said, “this is the first time I’ve played a solo concert all by myself.” Meaning that he had done solo concerts before but it was always on some kind of double bill. He might be the opening act and then there would be something. You know Normal Granz was his manager for a while, I mean he booked him during the Jazz at the Philharmonic days, so there were things like that. Or he would appear in concert with his trio. But he said this was the first time he had done — so that completely floored me. And that’s when I sort of started — not right away, but it started me thinking about trying to do something for this music. Because there was a © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-
genius like that and he was not adequately recognized. Tatum died a year later. He died in ’56.
